## Common Collocations
- **hacer la maleta** — to pack; literally "to make the suitcase"
- **hacer escala en** — to have a layover in; "Hicimos escala en Miami"
- **pasar por la aduana** — to go through customs; uses **por** (through)
- **viajar por** — to travel through/around; "Viajé por Europa" (C-05 reinforcement)
- **viajar para** — to travel to (destination); "Viajo para Madrid mañana"
- **ir de vacaciones** — to go on vacation; NOT "ir en vacaciones"
- **sacar fotos** — to take photos; also **tomar fotos**. NOT "hacer fotos" in Latin America (but Spain uses **hacer fotos**).
- **valer la pena** — to be worth it; "Vale la pena visitar ese museo"
- **quedarse en** — to stay at; "Nos quedamos en un hotel cerca de la playa"

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **el destino** vs **destiny**: **Destino** means both destination and destiny/fate. "¿Cuál es tu destino?" = "Where are you headed?" in a travel context.
- **el equipaje** vs **equipment**: **Equipaje** means luggage. Equipment is **el equipo** (which also means "team").
- **la estación** vs **station/season**: **Estación** means both. "La estación de tren" = train station. "Las cuatro estaciones" = the four seasons. Context determines meaning.
- **soportar** vs **support**: **Soportar** means to tolerate/endure. "No soporto el calor" = "I can't stand the heat." To support is **apoyar**.
- **el billete** vs **billet**: In Spain, **billete** means ticket AND banknote. A military billet would be **un acuartelamiento**.

## Dialect Variations
- **ticket**: **El boleto** (Latin America) vs **el billete** (Spain). In Spain, **billete** also means banknote.
- **reservation**: **La reservación** (Latin America) vs **la reserva** (Spain).
- **to take photos**: **Sacar fotos** (Latin America) vs **hacer fotos** (Spain). Both are immediately understood.
- **car**: **El carro** (Mexico, Caribbean, Central America) vs **el coche** (Spain) vs **el auto** (Southern Cone).
- **bus**: **El camión** (Mexico — also means "truck"), **el autobús** (Spain, universal), **el bus** (Colombia, widespread), **la guagua** (Cuba, Canary Islands — means "baby" elsewhere!), **el colectivo** (Argentina).
- **to miss (a place)**: **Extrañar** (Latin America) vs **echar de menos** (Spain).

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Por vs para in travel**: Travel vocabulary naturally forces por/para distinction. **Viajar por España** = travel through/around Spain. **Viajar para España** = travel toward Spain (destination). **Pagué mucho por el vuelo** = I paid a lot for the flight (exchange). **El regalo es para mi mamá** = The gift is for my mom (recipient). This cluster is ideal for reinforcing C-05.
- **Conditional for travel dreams**: "Viajaría a...", "Me gustaría conocer...", "Si pudiera, iría a..." — travel is the most natural context for conditional practice (C-04 reinforcement).
- **"Conocer" for first visits**: When visiting a place for the first time, Spanish uses **conocer**: "Quiero conocer París." Once you've been, subsequent visits use **visitar**: "Quiero visitar París otra vez."
- **Regional bus terminology**: Bus names vary wildly by country (see Dialect Variations). This is one of the most region-specific vocabulary areas in Spanish. When in doubt, **autobús** is universally understood.
- **Bargaining culture**: In markets and informal settings in Mexico and Central America, bargaining (**regatear**) is common and expected. "¿Cuánto cuesta?" followed by "¿Me hace un descuento?" is standard.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **equipaje** — stress on the third syllable: e-qui-PA-je. The **qu** is /k/, not /kw/.
- **aeropuerto** — five syllables: a-e-ro-PUER-to. Don't compress **a-e** into one syllable.
- **alojamiento** — stress on the fourth syllable: a-lo-ja-MIEN-to.
- **acogedor** — stress on the last syllable: a-co-ge-DOR. Not a-CO-ge-dor.
- **pintoresco** — stress on the third syllable: pin-to-RES-co.
- **paisaje** — three syllables: pai-SA-je. The **ai** diphthong is one syllable.
